outcome: The conjecture remains open. A June 2025 self-archived HAL preprint by Idriss Aberkane claims a full elementary proof, but it has received no expert digestion, no citations, no peer review, and no discussion in any mathematical venue I could find; its author has a well-documented history of discredited self-published claims to solve famous open problems (e.g. Collatz) in predatory venues. A March 2026 UBC seminar by Doug Lind and Mike Boyle produces counterexamples to a stronger variant of the conjecture (weak* convergence of ×3-iterates of a ×2-invariant continuous measure to Lebesgue), not to the original Furstenberg conjecture as stated in this bullet, so it is out of scope under §3.1. No AI involvement was found in any of this.
summary: The frozen bullet asks: is every invariant, ergodic measure for the ×2,×3 action on the circle either Lebesgue or atomic? I could not find any result since 26 January 2024 that changes what a careful person would write in this entry. The most up-to-date technical account is Matan Tal's survey (arXiv:2110.05989), whose v13 (17 Sep 2025) states the conjecture is still open in full generality, that 'contemporary knowledge... is more or less summarized by Rudolph's Theorem' (positive entropy case), and that 'not much is known about the case of zero entropy' — i.e. no narrowing of the survey's own account of the state of the art occurred in the window. The triage flagged a June 2025 HAL preprint by Idriss J. Aberkane, 'A Low-Tech Proof of Furstenberg's ×2–×3 Conjecture' (hal-05122193), which claims a complete elementary proof using Lucas's 2-adic congruence, binary digits of powers of 3 forming Sierpiński-gasket patterns, a finite-range cellular-automaton encoding, and entropy rigidity (Rudolph/Host). I was unable to open the PDF directly (it sits behind an Anubis bot-protection challenge on HAL and multiple fetch attempts, including a browser user-agent and a text-extraction proxy, were blocked), so I could not verify the argument or check for any AI-tool disclosure inside it; nothing in any secondary source or search result mentions AI involvement in this preprint. More importantly, I found zero evidence of any expert reading it: no citations, no MathOverflow or blog discussion, no journal submission, no rebuttal. That absence is itself informative given Aberkane's documented history — Wikipedia's own article on him records that he previously claimed to have solved the Collatz conjecture in a paper mathematicians say contains errors 'at the level of a high-school or first-year college student,' published in an MDPI journal described as predatory, and that a university sought to revoke his PhD for plagiarism. Under §6.1, a preprint with no digestion is at most `claimed`, and given the complete absence of any uptake at all (not even a critical response), and the author's track record, I judge the honest classification of this specific event to be indistinguishable from noise rather than a real claimed result worth elevating the status — so I record it as background context in this summary rather than as the decisive `event`, and keep `status` at `open`/`no_change_found`. I separately found a March 2026 seminar (UBC, speaker Doug Lind with Mike Boyle) building on 2024-era work by Badea and Grivaux that produces counterexamples to a *stronger* variant of the conjecture (about weak* convergence of ×3-pushforwards of a ×2-invariant continuous measure to Lebesgue measure), explicitly framed by the speaker as not resolving the classical Furstenberg conjecture. Per §3.1 that is a related/variant problem, not a case of this one, so it does not count as a change here. I also checked the current Wikipedia articles for Hillel Furstenberg and the 'List of unsolved problems' entry itself; neither reflects any resolution or update. No Lean/Coq formalisation effort, lab announcement, or AI system's involvement with this specific conjecture turned up in any search.
competing_reading: One could argue the Aberkane preprint should be coded as `claimed` (a preprint that experts have not yet digested) purely because it exists and explicitly claims to resolve the exact bullet. Weighing against this: a `claimed` status implies a serious claim in circulation, and this preprint shows no signs of having entered circulation at all (zero citations, zero discussion anywhere I could search), combined with the author's well-documented pattern of self-published, mathematically flawed 'solutions' to famous problems posted to preprint servers without peer review. If a future pass can access the PDF directly and confirms the argument is at least superficially serious (uses real, checkable machinery rather than being obviously circular or vacuous), the correct call would shift to `claimed`, dated June 2025.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the HAL PDF (currently blocked by bot protection) to assess whether the proof is a serious, checkable attempt or an obvious non-proof; any expert commentary, rebuttal, or citation of the Aberkane preprint; confirmation of whether it was ever submitted to or rejected by a journal.
